analysis.investment_thesis: MOIL is a PSU commodity miner — the polar opposite of what I look for. Despite zero debt, ROE of 8.3% and flat net profit over a decade (₹428 Cr in 2015 vs ₹382 Cr in 2025) tell the story of a business that destroys time-value of capital.
key_strengths: Zero debt across entire history — balance sheet is pristine and fully equity-funded
Government promoter at 64.68% ensures near-monopoly in Indian manganese mining
OCF positive in all 5 of the last 5 years, showing operational cash generation
key_risks: Commodity cyclicality makes earnings wildly volatile — net profit swings from ₹173 Cr (2016) to ₹478 Cr (2019) to ₹251 Cr (2023) with no control over pricing
ROE of only 8.31% and ROCE of 11.4% are well below my 15% minimum — capital is not being deployed productively
Current P/E of 64.2x for a cyclical PSU miner with flat 10-year earnings is completely unjustifiable — forward P/E of 12.6x implies an earnings surge that is unproven
red_flags: 10-year revenue CAGR of ~6.7% (₹822 Cr in 2015 → ₹1,579 Cr in 2025) — well below my 10-15% steady growth requirement
FCF negative in 3 of last 5 years (2020, 2023, 2024) as capex eats into operating cash; FCF yield barely 2% in FY25
PSU governance — government as promoter means sub-optimal capital allocation, bureaucratic decision-making, and no alignment with minority shareholders
Other income (treasury income) contracting at -10.6% CAGR — historically this subsidized reported profits, masking weak core business returns
analysis.detailed_analysis:
MOIL is fundamentally outside my investment universe — it is a commodity miner, not a consumer business. I built DMart on the principle that businesses serving daily, non-discretionary human needs compound wealth reliably. Manganese ore prices are set by global steel cycles, not by brand, loyalty, or repeat purchase behaviour. The earnings history confirms this: operating income collapsed from ₹600 Cr (FY19) to ₹264 Cr (FY23), a 56% drop in four years, purely on commodity price weakness. No amount of management skill can offset this structural volatility, and that is precisely the kind of business I avoid.

The financial metrics reinforce the AVOID call across every dimension I care about. ROE of 8.31% means the business earns less than a fixed deposit on its equity book. The P/E of 64x is absurd for a cyclical commodity company — this is a speculative price reflecting hope of a manganese price upcycle, not a quality business at a fair price. The only genuine virtue here is zero debt, which I respect deeply, but a pristine balance sheet cannot compensate for a business that earns low returns on capital, has no pricing power, and has delivered flat absolute profits over ten years. I would rather hold cash than buy this.
